# Short answer

For most full-size fridges, a station with about 1,000 Wh covers roughly half a day to a day. About 2,000 Wh gives you a full day with margin. Make sure its surge rating is at least about 1,300 W and that it has pure sine wave output.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Surge watts:** This is the spec that most often fails. The compressor briefly draws about 1,000-2,400 W at startup, depending on fridge size ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). One guide uses 1,300 W as a safe allowance ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). A station with plenty of Wh can still trip at startup if its surge rating is too low.
2. **Continuous watts:** A full-size fridge runs at about 100-250 W, which almost any 1,000 W-class station handles.
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time. A typical fridge averages roughly 40-70 W, or about 1,000 Wh per day. Adding inverter losses and headroom brings that to about 1,400 Wh per day ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

## Rough sizing

| Outage length | Capacity to look for |
|---|---|
| ~12-16 hours | ~1,000 Wh |
| 24 hours | ~1,400-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh or more |

Runtimes are estimates, since door openings, a warm kitchen, an ice maker and an older fridge all raise consumption. For a precise number, check your fridge's EnergyGuide label (kWh/year ÷ 8,760 × 1,000 = average watts) or the DOE's rating search tool ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)). Keeping the door shut helps a lot.

## Options that fit

- **About 1,000 Wh (half a day to a day):** The [BLUETTI AC180](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) has 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W continuous and 2,700 W peak, at about $399-699 recently. The [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) is listed at about 17 hours of fridge runtime for $499.
- **About 2,000 Wh (a full day or more):**
  - [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) has 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous and 3,600 W surge. It's rated for about 33 hours on a fridge ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)) and can expand up to 8 kWh. The store price is $899, or $854.05 with code AFF5OFF, which was tested in BLUETTI's cart on 2026-10-21. The checkout price is the final word. This is an affiliate link, so Dealectric earns a commission at no cost to you ([details](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l)).
  - [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) has 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W continuous and 3,000 W peak, listed at $699.99 after coupon.

The Anker S2000 is the cheapest of the 2 kWh-class options listed here, and the AC200L is the one to pick if you may want to expand later. If your outages are short and you mainly want to protect a fridge's contents overnight, the 1,000 Wh class is enough. If you also want lights, a router or a phone charger, or you're in an area with long outages, go to 2,000 Wh or more.

Let me know your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year figure and how long your outages typically last, and I can narrow it down.
